unit.title: Manage intellectual property to protect and grow business

summary: This unit teaches managers to protect and grow a business through its intellectual property. You will learn to build an IP strategy from the business goals, audit and value IP, choose and time protection, license or sell IP, budget and measure results, monitor and enforce rights and prepare IP for investors and lenders.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for managers and owners of Jamaican businesses, agencies and institutions who must decide how the firm's ideas, names, designs, recipes, software and know-how are to be **protected** and how they can be used to **grow** the business. **Intellectual property (IP)** means creations of the mind that the law lets the owner control: inventions, brand names, designs, written and musical works, software and confidential know-how.

IP is often the most valuable thing a small firm owns, yet it is the thing most often left unmanaged. A manager does not need to be a lawyer. A manager does need to know what the firm owns, what it risks, what protection is worth paying for, how to earn money from IP, and when to call an IP attorney or the Jamaica Intellectual Property Office (JIPO). This kit follows the order of the work: strategy, audit and valuation, choosing protection, commercialising, budgeting and measuring, enforcing and managing risk, and finally innovation and investors.

What this means in your unit

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with many short scenarios and sums.
A written paper with short answers (exact terms such as FTO, licensee, priority date) and longer answers where you advise on a strategy, a choice of protection or a licensing deal.
Group practical tasks: an IP strategy and budget for an export launch, and an appraisal of ways to commercialise a patented invention.

blocks.note: Many questions include a sum (royalties, budgets, payback, percentages). Work every sum twice and write the unit (J$, %, years).

sections.title: IP strategy: starting from the business goals

blocks.p: An **IP strategy** is the firm's plan for using IP to reach its business goals. It is not a list of everything the firm could register. It answers four questions: what do we own or create, what matters most to our income, how will we protect and use it, and who is responsible?

The strategy is **built around the business plan**: the products, the markets, the partners and the growth the firm wants. A hot-sauce maker planning to export to three countries needs trade marks in those countries before launch. A firm that will never leave Jamaica does not need to spend on foreign filings. The purpose of managing IP is to **gain an edge and earn income**, not to collect certificates and not to treat IP as a legal cost to cut.

head: Kind of IP
What it protects
Key points for a manager
rows: Patent
A new, inventive technical solution (a product or a process)

Must be new when filed, so file before any public showing. Gives a limited period of exclusive rights, usually up to about 20 years from filing. The invention is published. Valid only in the countries where granted.
Trade mark
Names, logos, slogans and other signs that tell customers who the goods or services come from

Registered for a set period and renewable. Covers only the goods and services listed. Can be lost if not used for a long time. A certification mark shows that goods meet a standard set by the mark owner.
Industrial design
The look of a product: shape, pattern, ornament
Must be new when filed. Protects appearance, not how the product works. Limited, renewable term.
Copyright
Original written, musical, artistic and recorded works, and software
Arises automatically when the work is created; registration is not needed to own it, though records of dates and authors help. Protects the expression, not the idea.
Trade secret (confidential information)
Recipes, formulas, methods, customer lists and know-how
Protected only while it stays secret, by controls and by confidentiality agreements. Lost if a rival works it out lawfully or it leaks.
Geographical indication or collective mark
The name of a place linked with a quality of goods
Used by a group of producers who meet agreed rules. Needs a body that sets and checks the rules.

blocks.note: Registered rights (patents, trade marks, designs) are **territorial**: a Jamaican registration protects the firm in Jamaica only. Protection in Barbados, Canada or the United Kingdom must be applied for there, through each country's office or an international route. Copyright is different, because it is recognised across many countries under international agreements.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Writing the strategy: a chain of steps

flow: Read the business plan: products, markets, partners, growth goals
List the IP the firm owns, uses and is creating, and confirm who owns it
Link each item to the products and income it supports
Check the risks: copying, other people's rights, gaps in ownership
Choose the protection and the markets for each item, with a timeline
Set the budget and the measures of success
Name the accountable manager, report to the board and review

blocks.p: IP needs an owner inside the firm. In a growing firm this is **a named senior manager who reports to the board** (in a small firm, the owner or general manager), supported by an IP attorney or agent. Without one, renewals are missed, products are launched without checks and nobody can say what the firm owns. The strategy should also set a simple **IP policy** for staff: ideas are reported, records are kept, confidential material is protected and nobody signs an agreement that gives away IP without approval.

blocks.note: A firm in Portland that makes seasoning blends has three kinds of IP in one jar: the **name and label** (trade mark and copyright), the **jar shape** (design) and the **blend** (trade secret). One strategy decides how each is protected.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: You cannot manage what you cannot see. An **IP audit** records every item of IP, then links it to income and to risk. The result is an **IP register**, kept up to date and reviewed each year.

head: Column in the register
Why it is there
rows: What the item is (name, description)
So everyone knows exactly what is covered
Type of right and where it is registered
Shows territories and gaps
Registration or application number and dates
Needed for renewals and proof
Owner (the company, a founder, a partner?)
Rights held in the wrong name cause trouble in sales and loans
Renewal date and cost
Prevents a **lapse** (the right ends because a fee was not paid)
Products and income it supports
Shows which IP matters most
Licences granted or taken, and disputes
Shows who else has rights

blocks.p: To find which IP drives revenue, **link each item to the products and income it supports**. Rank by income and by risk. A logo used on every product matters more than an old design for a product no longer sold.
Ownership is a common weak point. As a general rule (confirm with an attorney):

ul: **Staff:** what an employee creates in the course of employment normally belongs to the employer. Say so in the employment contract, for clarity.

**Freelancers, consultants and agencies:** they usually keep the rights in what they create unless a **written assignment** passes them to the firm. A firm that paid a freelancer to write its software, design its logo or take its photographs may not own them.
**Founders:** anything created before the company was formed belongs to the founder until it is formally assigned to the company.
**Joint work with partners or universities:** the agreement must say who owns the results and who may use them.

blocks.note: Ask for a signed **assignment** (a written transfer of ownership) every time an outsider creates something the firm will rely on. A buyer, lender or investor will ask to see it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Managers value IP to decide how much to spend on it, to set licence fees, to support a loan and to price the business. There are three approaches.

head: Approach
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Cost
What it cost to create, or would cost to replace
Uses figures that are easy to find
Cost often has little link to value
Market
Prices paid for similar IP in sales or licences
Reflects what buyers pay
Comparable deals are rare and rarely public
Income
The future earnings the IP is expected to bring, brought back to today's value
Links value to earnings
Depends on forecasts and on the rate chosen

blocks.p: **Relief from royalty** is an income method. It asks: what royalty would the firm have to pay if it did not own the brand and had to license it? The royalty it saves each year by owning it is the benefit.

head: Step
Worked example
rows: 1. Forecast the sales the brand supports
2. Choose a fair royalty rate from similar licences
6% of sales
3. Royalty saved each year
4. Add up over the years the brand will last (simple version)
Four years: J$12,000,000
5. In a full valuation, discount future years to today's value
At 10% a year, J$3,000,000 for 3 years is worth about J$7.46 million today

blocks.p: Check of step 5: 3,000,000 ÷ 1.10 = 2,727,273; ÷ 1.21 = 2,479,339; ÷ 1.331 = 2,253,942; total about J$7,460,554. Discounting reflects that money received later is worth less than money in hand now. A valuer or accountant should set the rate.

blocks.note: A bank that lends against IP, such as a catalogue of song copyrights, will want two things: a **sound valuation** and **proof that the borrower owns the IP**. The IP is then offered as **collateral** (security for the loan).
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Choosing protection: type, timing and place

blocks.p: The right protection depends on the asset, how easily it can be copied, how long it will stay valuable, and how much the firm can spend.

head: Question
If the answer is yes
rows: Can a rival work out the method by examining the product once it is on sale?
Secrecy will fail. A patent is the better choice.
Can the firm control who sees the method (few staff, strong agreements)?
Secrecy is possible and costs less.
Will the advantage last longer than about 20 years?
Secrecy has no time limit, but only while it stays secret.
Does the firm want to license it, sell it or attract investors?
A patent is a clear asset that can be shown, licensed and sold.
Is the improvement small, easy to design around, or out of date within a year?
Record it, but do not pay to patent it.

blocks.p: A patent buys exclusive rights in return for **publishing** the invention. When the patent ends, anyone may use the invention. A trade secret reveals nothing, but it gives no protection against a rival who discovers it independently.

head: Asset
Usual protection
rows: Brand name and logo
Trade mark in each market
Label artwork, website text, photographs
Copyright (automatic); keep records of the creator and date
Shape or pattern of a product
Design registration, where copying is a risk
New technical feature
Patent, if new and worth the cost
Recipe or process that cannot be seen in the product
Trade secret with strict controls
A mark used by many makers that pass a quality check
Certification mark owned by the association that sets the standard

blocks.p: A patent or design must usually be **new** at the filing date. Showing the product at a trade fair, selling a first batch, posting it online or letting an outsider test it before filing can destroy novelty. The rule is: **protect first, then show**. For a design to be shown at a fair in Kingston or Miami, file before the fair.

The date of the first filing is the **priority date**. Under international agreements, an applicant who files in other member countries within a set time may rely on that first date. The usual periods are about **12 months for patents and 6 months for trade marks and designs**. Treat these as dates to diarise and confirm with the attorney.

Few firms can afford every market. Rank markets by **current and planned sales, the risk of copying and the cost**, then register in the top ones first. A brand known abroad but registered only in Jamaica faces the biggest risk: **someone else may register it first** in that market and block the owner.

Owning a registration does not mean the firm may use the product. Another firm's earlier right may block it. A **freedom to operate (FTO)** search checks whether the product can be made and sold without infringing other people's rights. For a brand, a **clearance search** looks for earlier marks that are identical or similar. Do it **before** spending money on launch, printing and packaging.

flow: Search for earlier marks, patents and designs in each market
Review the results with the attorney and decide whether the name or product can be used
File the applications and record the priority date
Launch only after filing (search, file, then launch)

blocks.note: A J$12,000,000 launch can be wasted if the name must be dropped after launch. A clearance search costs a small fraction of that.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Commercialising IP: making money from what you own

blocks.p: IP can earn income in several ways. The choice depends on the firm's money, skills, speed and appetite for risk.

head: Option
What it means
Gains
Risks
rows: Make and sell it yourself
The firm manufactures and markets the product
All the profit and full control
Needs capital, premises, staff and market access
Licence it
The owner keeps ownership and gives another party permission to use it, for fees and royalties
Income with little capital; ownership kept; reaches new markets
A weak licensee; the cost of monitoring
Assign (sell) it
Ownership passes to the buyer outright
Quick lump sum, low risk
All future income and control are gone; may be sold too cheaply
Joint venture
Two firms combine IP and resources, often in a new company
Shared cost and risk; access to a partner's market
Complex to set up; disagreements are hard to settle
Spin-off
A new company is set up to develop and sell the IP
Lets a larger firm or university release value from IP outside its main business
Needs management and funding
Franchise
The brand, system and know-how are licensed to operators who follow set standards
Fast growth using others' capital
Quality control and support are demanding

head: Term
Why it matters
rows: Parties: licensor (owner) and licensee (receiver)
The licence names exactly who may use the IP
Scope: which IP, which products, which territory, which field
Prevents use outside what was agreed
Exclusive, sole or non-exclusive
**Exclusive:** only the licensee may use it, even the owner may not. **Sole:** the licensee and the owner only. **Non-exclusive:** the owner may license others.
Fees: upfront fee, royalty (a percentage of net sales or a sum per unit)
Defines the owner's income
**Minimum yearly royalty**
Protects the owner if the licensee sells little
Quality standards and approval of samples
Protects the brand
Right to inspect the sales records (audit)
Lets the owner check that royalties are paid correctly
Improvements: who owns them
A licensee should try to secure rights in improvements it makes itself
Term and termination
Sets the length and the events (non-payment, missed targets) that end it
Sub-licensing, assignment, governing law, dispute method
Controls who else may become involved

blocks.p: A licensee will pay an upfront fee of J$1,800,000 and a royalty of 5% of net sales. Expected sales are J$40,000,000 a year for three years.

ul: Royalty over three years: 3 × J$2,000,000 = J$6,000,000

blocks.p: Check: 40,000,000 × 0.05 = 2,000,000; × 3 = 6,000,000; + 1,800,000 = 7,800,000. Note that this is expected income, not guaranteed income. A minimum yearly royalty would make part of it certain.

ul: **Cross-licensing:** two firms license each other, which reduces disputes and cost.
**Patent pool:** several owners agree to license related patents together as one package.
**Open innovation:** working with outside partners, such as universities and start-ups, to share ideas and develop products faster. Agreements must say who owns what.
**Licensing in:** the firm takes a licence of someone else's technology. A Jamaican manufacturer should negotiate for rights to its own improvements, a fair territory and terms that let it grow.
**Collateral:** IP offered to a lender as security. The lender needs a valuation and proof of ownership.

blocks.note: A small Jamaican firm with a good patent but little capital usually does best by **licensing for royalties**, preferably by territory, with a minimum royalty, quality standards, audit rights and the right to end the licence if targets are missed.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Budgeting, cost and benefit, and measuring results

blocks.p: IP costs money every year: searches, filing fees, attorneys' fees, renewals, watch services and enforcement. A manager plans these costs like any other budget, and compares them with the benefit.

head: Line
Example
rows: Jamaica trade mark filing
Five export markets at J$180,000 each (search and filing)
Total filing budget
Renewals due: 24 marks at an average J$45,000
Watch service and contingency
Set a sum for monitoring and for unexpected advice

blocks.p: Show the budget by **year** and by **market**, and add a contingency. Do the totals twice, once across and once down.
Compare what protection costs with the extra profit it is expected to protect.

head: Method
Worked example
rows: Net benefit = extra profit from protection minus its cost

Protecting a design costs J$2,100,000 over five years. Without protection, copies are expected to cut profit by J$500,000 a year. Benefit: 5 × J$500,000 = J$2,500,000. Net benefit: J$2,500,000 − J$2,100,000 = **J$400,000**.
Payback (years) = cost ÷ extra profit each year
Coverage = income ÷ cost
IP costs J$1,500,000 a year and licensing earns J$6,000,000: 6,000,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = **4 times**.
Share of revenue from protected products
Revenue J$150,000,000, of which J$45,000,000 is from protected products: 45 ÷ 150 = **30%**.

blocks.p: Test the assumptions. A forecast benefit holds only if protection really stops copying, which depends on the firm being willing and able to enforce it. Ask how fast past products were copied, how long the product will stay popular, and whether protecting only the largest markets would cut the cost.

ul: Share of revenue from protected products
Licensing income, and licensing income compared with IP costs
IP spending compared with budget
Renewals met on time (the target is all of them)
New rights filed, and new products that passed IP checks before launch
Infringements found and resolved
Coming renewals and the cost of the next quarter

blocks.p: A **quarterly IP report** to the board should include income, costs, risks and coming renewals. The strategy itself is reviewed **at set times (for example every year) and whenever the business changes**, such as a new market, a new product line or a licence ending.
A right that is never watched is easily lost in practice. Monitoring finds problems early, and a planned response keeps enforcement affordable.

ul: **Trade mark watch service:** alerts the firm when someone applies for a similar mark.
**Staff and distributors:** ask them to report copies and send photographs.
**Online checks:** marketplaces, social media and domain names.
**Competitor patents:** studying the patents a rival has filed shows where it is investing.
**Log every report** with dates, photographs and purchases as evidence.

flow: Rank the case: the market, the sales at risk, the strength of the right
Send a formal letter, then negotiate (a settlement, perhaps a licence, is often the fastest and cheapest outcome)
Use takedown requests for online sellers; consider mediation
Keep court action for serious cases

blocks.p: Weigh **the cost of action against the likely harm**. A small problem in a market where the firm does not trade and has no plans may need only monitoring. A copy in a key market needs prompt action. Be careful not to make unfounded threats; get advice before writing.

A registered trade mark that is not used for a long period can be removed. Keep using marks in trade, and review ones that no longer matter. Pay renewal fees on time: an unpaid fee means the right **lapses**.
List each IP risk, score the **likelihood** and the **impact** (for example 1 to 5 each), multiply to get a rating, then assign an action and an owner.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Rating
Action
rows: Core software relies on a licence that ends next year
Open renewal talks now; plan an alternative
Brand registered only in Jamaica but sold in two markets
File in both markets; set priority
Freelancer wrote the app code, no assignment
Obtain a signed assignment
Renewal date missed for a key mark
Diarise dates with two reminders

blocks.p: Rating = likelihood × impact: 4 × 5 = 20, 3 × 4 = 12, 3 × 5 = 15, 2 × 5 = 10. Deal with the highest ratings first.

blocks.note: A risk register entry needs an action and a named owner. A list of worries with no actions is not a register.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: IP in innovation, investment and growth

blocks.h: IP checks at every stage of product development

head: Stage
IP action
rows: Idea
Record ideas with dates and names; keep them confidential
Early research
Search patents, designs and marks: is it new, and could other rights block it?
Design and development
Keep dated records; contractors and partners sign confidentiality and ownership agreements
Before any public showing
File for patent or design protection first
Branding
Clear and register the name and logo in the launch markets
Before launch
Check that all outside software, images and music are licensed
After launch
Monitor for copies, renew, update the register

blocks.p: Building checks into each stage means IP is **caught and protected as it arises**. Encourage staff to report ideas by making reporting easy and **rewarding useful ideas**.

ul: A firm with a strong registered mark for coffee that plans to sell mugs and T-shirts under the same name should first check **whether its registration covers those goods**. Marks cover only the goods and services listed.
A family firm planning to sell in five years raises its sale value most by **registering its IP and making clear who owns it**.
A firm that sells downloadable training videos protects its income with **access controls and licensed user accounts**.

blocks.h: Investors, lenders and buyers: due diligence

blocks.p: **Due diligence** is the careful investigation a buyer or investor makes of a firm before a deal. They check IP closely because much of a modern firm's value rests on it. Prepare in advance.

ul: Prepare an IP schedule listing every item, its owner, registration status and renewal dates.
Confirm signed assignments from founders, staff and freelancers.
Check that registrations are in the company's name, not a founder's.
List outside and open-source software and confirm the licence terms are met, because some licences limit how the product may be sold.
Collect all licences granted or received, and any disputes or warnings.
Put the documents in a secure data room and be ready to explain how the IP supports the business plan.

blocks.note: If main software was written by a freelancer without a written transfer of rights, the firm may **not own the software it sells**. Fix this with a written assignment before due diligence, not during it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain what an IP strategy is and build one around the firm's business goals, with a named accountable manager.
name the main kinds of IP and say what each protects and how long it lasts in general terms.
build an IP register and link each item to the products and income it supports.
explain who owns IP created by staff, freelancers and founders, and why written assignments matter.
explain cost, market and income valuation, and work a relief-from-royalty example.
decide between a patent and a trade secret and give reasons.
explain why a firm must file before showing a product, and what a priority date is.
carry out the steps of clearance and freedom to operate before launch.
compare making, licensing, assigning, joint ventures and spin-offs, and name the licence terms to negotiate.
work out total licence income, budgets, net benefit, payback, coverage and share of revenue from protected products.
set up monitoring, rank infringement cases and choose a proportionate response.
build an IP risk register with ratings and actions.
build IP checks into each stage of product development.
prepare a firm's IP for due diligence by an investor, lender or buyer.

terms: Creations of the mind that the law lets the owner control.
The whole set of IP rights a firm holds and manages together.
The firm's up-to-date list of its IP with owners, dates and costs.
Exclusive right to a new, inventive technical solution for a limited period, in return for publishing it.
A sign that tells customers who goods or services come from.
A mark any maker may use if its goods meet the standard set by the mark owner.
Automatic protection of original written, musical, artistic and recorded works.
Confidential know-how protected while it stays secret.
A check that a product can be made and sold without infringing other people's rights.
The date of the first filing, which can be relied on when filing abroad within the set period.
Outright transfer of ownership of an IP right.
Permission to use IP; the owner who gives it; the party who receives it.
A payment for the use of IP, usually a percentage of sales or a sum per unit.
The least the licensee must pay each year.
Valuing IP by the royalty saved by owning it.
A buyer's or investor's detailed check of a firm, including its IP.
An asset pledged to a lender as security for a loan.

c1.title: Rushworth Foods, Portland
c1.text: Rushworth Foods, a family firm in Portland, makes a jerk seasoning that sells well in Jamaica. It will launch the product under the name "Blue Hole Jerk" in Barbados, Canada and the United Kingdom within 18 months. The brand is registered in Jamaica only. The seasoning blend cannot be identified by tasting or testing the finished product. The managing director, Mrs Charmaine Bryan, will present the IP plan to the board. Filing and search together cost J$180,000 for each export market, and the Jamaican registration is already paid up.

c2.title: Norwood Furniture, Spanish Town
c2.text: Norwood Furniture has created a stackable chair with a distinctive shape that is selling well to restaurants. Owner Mr Dwight Norwood expects copies from importers within a year. Registering and defending the design in its main markets would cost J$3,000,000 over six years. With protection, the firm expects extra profit of J$1,100,000 a year. Without it, the firm expects extra profit of J$500,000 a year. The chair is to be shown at a trade fair in Port of Spain in six weeks.

c3.title: Greenfield Valve, Mandeville
c3.text: Greenfield Valve holds a Jamaican patent on a water-saving irrigation valve. It has little capital to build a factory. A manufacturer in Trinidad offers a non-exclusive licence for the Caribbean: an upfront fee of J$1,500,000 and a royalty of 4% of net sales. The licensee expects sales of J$35,000,000 in year 1 and J$50,000,000 in year 2. Greenfield's managing director, Ms Andrea Facey, wants a minimum royalty of J$1,800,000 a year and the right to inspect the licensee's sales records.

c4.title: Island Roots Records, Kingston
c4.text: Island Roots Records owns a catalogue of 120 songs and wants a bank loan secured on it. The catalogue earns J$24,000,000 a year. Similar catalogues are licensed at a royalty of about 12% of income. During the bank's review, the finance manager, Mr Orville Grant, finds that nine songs were written by freelance songwriters who never signed a transfer of rights. He also finds that four trade marks for the label's name are registered in the name of the founder, not the company.

c5.title: Cool Spring Beverages, Portmore
c5.text: Cool Spring Beverages holds 40 registered trade marks. Renewal costs an average of J$38,000 a mark. A review by IP manager Ms Shanique Reid shows that 12 of the marks are for drinks discontinued years ago. Last year revenue was J$210,000,000, of which J$126,000,000 came from protected products. The firm spent J$1,500,000 on IP management and earned J$3,000,000 from licensing a mark to a bottler in Guyana. A watch service reports that a firm in Trinidad has applied to register a mark very like "Cool Spring Zero".

questions.q: Mrs Bryan is asked what the IP strategy should be built around. Which is the best answer?
o: The IP strategies of the largest food companies in each market
The lowest registration fees that can be found in each market
The export plan: its products, markets and launch dates
A list of every name the firm has ever thought of using
questions.why: An IP strategy exists to support the business plan. Here the export launch decides which marks, in which markets and when. Copying other firms' strategies or minimising fees ignores the firm's own goals.

questions.q: The blend cannot be identified by tasting the finished seasoning. How should Rushworth protect the blend?
o: As a trade secret, with controls and signed agreements
With a patent, so that rivals cannot copy the blend
With a trade mark, because the blend is part of the brand
With a design registration, because the blend is distinctive
questions.why: A recipe that cannot be worked out from the product can stay secret at no filing cost and with no time limit. A patent would publish it, and trade marks and designs protect names and appearance, not recipes.

questions.q: What should the firm do before it spends money on labels and packaging for "Blue Hole Jerk" in the UK?
o: Print the labels first so that unit costs are known
Ask buyers in each market whether they like the name
Renew the Jamaican registration to refresh its date
Search for earlier marks that could block the name
questions.why: A clearance search is done before launch costs are incurred. If an earlier mark blocks the name, the firm can change it before printing and packaging are wasted.

questions.q: What is the total budget for searching and filing in the three export markets?
questions.why: 3 × J$180,000 = J$540,000. The Jamaican registration is already paid, so it is not added. Checking: 180,000 × 3 = 540,000.

questions.q: Mr Norwood plans to show the chair at the trade fair in six weeks. When should he apply to register the design?
o: At the fair, if visitors admire it
Before the fair, while the design is still new
After the fair, once he knows buyers are interested
Only when a copy appears on the market
questions.why: A design usually must be new when filed. Showing it publicly first can destroy that novelty. File before the fair and then show it.

questions.q: Over six years, what is the net benefit of protecting the design, compared with not protecting it?
questions.why: The extra profit from protection is J$1,100,000 − J$500,000 = J$600,000 a year, which is J$3,600,000 over six years. Subtract the J$3,000,000 cost to get J$600,000.

questions.q: How many years will it take for the extra profit from protection to repay its cost?
o: 5 years
3 years
6 years
2 years
questions.why: Protection adds J$600,000 a year (1,100,000 − 500,000). The cost of J$3,000,000 ÷ J$600,000 = 5 years. Payback is cost divided by the extra profit each year.

questions.q: Before relying on the J$1,100,000 forecast, what is the most important check?
o: Whether the chair could also be made in other colours
Whether the registration papers are filed in good order
Whether the firm can and will enforce it in each market
Whether competing makers also attend the trade fair
questions.why: The protected profit only exists if the design actually stops copying, which depends on enforcement. A forecast that ignores this may be too hopeful.

questions.q: What are the royalties on the Trinidad firm's expected sales in years 1 and 2 combined?
questions.why: Royalty = 4% of sales. Year 1: J$1,400,000. Year 2: J$2,000,000. Total J$3,400,000. J$4,900,000 would wrongly include the upfront fee.

questions.q: The licensee asks for an exclusive licence for the Caribbean instead. What would this mean for Greenfield?
o: It could license other firms but not sell valves itself
It could not license anyone else in the Caribbean
It would give up ownership of the patent to the licensee
It would lose the right to receive any royalty on sales
questions.why: An exclusive licence means only the licensee may use the patent in the licensed territory, so the owner cannot license others there (and, unless the licence says otherwise, cannot use it either). Ownership and royalties stay with the owner.

questions.q: Why does Ms Facey ask for a minimum royalty of J$1,800,000 a year?
o: It lets the licensee sell as much as it wishes without limit
It transfers ownership of the patent once it has been paid
It protects Greenfield's income if the licensee sells little
It guarantees that every valve will meet quality checks
questions.why: If sales are low, the 4% royalty could be small. A minimum yearly royalty gives the owner a floor and gives the licensee a reason to promote the product.

questions.q: The licensee may improve the valve design during the licence. What should Greenfield's licence say about improvements?
o: Who owns them, and that Greenfield may also use them
Nothing, because improvements always belong to the patent owner
That the licensee owns them and Greenfield may never use them
That improvements must be kept secret from Greenfield
questions.why: Ownership of improvements is a negotiated term. Without a clause, disputes follow. Greenfield should settle who owns them and secure the right to use them, while the licensee will want rights in its own work.

questions.q: Using relief from royalty, how much does owning the catalogue save the company each year?
questions.why: Royalty saved = 12% of J$24,000,000 = J$2,880,000 a year. J$14,400,000 would be five years of savings, not one.

questions.q: Nine songs were written by freelancers who never signed a transfer of rights. What should Mr Grant recommend?
o: Leave the matter, since copyright needs no paperwork to be owned
Tell the bank only if it asks about the nine songs in particular
Get signed assignments from the songwriters before applying
Treat the songs as owned because the company paid for recordings
questions.why: Freelance creators usually keep their rights unless these are transferred in writing. The bank needs proof of ownership, so the gap should be fixed first.

questions.q: Four trade marks for the label's name are registered in the founder's name. What is the sound solution?
o: Keep them in the founder's name and mention it to the bank
Record the transfer of the registrations to the company
Re-register new marks under a slightly different name
Allow the marks to lapse and rely on copyright
questions.why: Rights held in the wrong name cause trouble in loans and sales. A written transfer, recorded with the registry, puts the marks where they belong.

questions.q: What will the bank most need to see before it accepts the catalogue as collateral?
o: A list of all the artists who have recorded the songs
The label's sales figures for its first three years
A forecast of how many new songs it will release
A sound valuation and proof of ownership
questions.why: A lender needs to know what the security is worth and that the borrower can really pledge it. Valuation and proof of ownership answer those two questions.

questions.q: Ms Reid recommends dropping or selling the 12 unused marks. What will the firm save in renewal fees each renewal cycle?
questions.why: 12 × J$38,000 = J$456,000. The total for 40 marks is J$1,520,000, and the 28 that remain cost J$1,064,000.

questions.q: What share of Cool Spring's revenue comes from protected products?
questions.why: 126,000,000 ÷ 210,000,000 = 0.6, so 60%. Share of revenue from protected products is a key measure of whether IP is helping the business.

questions.q: The firm spent J$1,500,000 on IP management and earned J$3,000,000 from licensing. How many times does the income cover the cost?
o: 4 times
0.5 times
1.5 times
2 times
questions.why: 3,000,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 2. Coverage is income divided by cost.

questions.q: The watch service reports a Trinidad application for a mark very like "Cool Spring Zero". What should management do first?
o: Ignore it, because the firm already owns its marks in Jamaica
Stop selling "Cool Spring Zero" in Jamaica until it is resolved
Take advice and weigh the Trinidad market against the cost
Apply at once to register the Trinidad firm's own business name
questions.why: A Jamaican registration does not protect the firm in Trinidad. The firm should weigh its sales and plans there against the cost of action, with legal advice, before opposing or negotiating.
